rationale:
Today qualifies as a Lane C news day. Lilly's TRANSCEND-T2D-2 topline came out on Oct 28, inside the 48-hour window. It is the first randomized Phase 3 head-to-head of retatrutide against another incretin, it reports headline efficacy numbers, and it has a semaglutide 2 mg arm. That fits every Exp C rule and the EloraTZP pattern behind about 54% of our watch time.

To keep the long-form verifiable, the news goes in the first 15 seconds only. The body rests on settled, peer-reviewed evidence:
- how a triple GIP/GLP-1/glucagon agonist works
- TRIUMPH-2 and TRANSCEND-T2D-1 (both in The Lancet)
- why people with type 2 diabetes lose less weight in every trial of this drug class

The new trial's figures are labelled company-reported, open-label, 'if everyone stayed on treatment' and not yet peer-reviewed. The side effects are given in full, and the dated status line says it is investigational.

Shorts:
- **08:00:** a calm body-worry Short with tirzepatide in the title. It leads with the pancreas, using the Oct 23 scoping review, so it doesn't repeat the 10-26 gallbladder Short.
- **13:00:** a deviation from the usual menu, made on purpose. No new two-drug trial with tirzepatide named first is available (SURMOUNT-5, SURPASS-2 and SURPASS-CVOT were all used recently). There's no new dated gray-market fact either. And a retatrutide Short here would break the one-trial-per-week Short rule, because the 20:00 funnel already uses TRANSCEND-T2D-2. So 13:00 is a rising, Halloween-timed food noise Short on tirzepatide (Psychiatric Times, Oct 28), framed as a gentle myth correction: biology, not willpower.
- **20:00:** the Exp D funnel Short and spin-off of L1. It asks one fresh question the long-form answers, about dysesthesia, the side-effect signal headlines skipped. It gives that trial its only Short this week.

Mix: 2 rising, 1 emerging, plus a myth-correction framing on the food noise piece. No carousels (quota 0).

Pillars: research ×2, get-the-most, how-it-works. Body systems are spread across metabolic and blood sugar, pancreas, brain and appetite, and nerves and skin sensation.

Nothing on the radar was marked reject. The 'caution' topics (stopping, birth control, pregnancy, thyroid) are left for other days. Protein and stopping stay next in the Lane A queue for tomorrow.

pieces.topic: Retatrutide vs semaglutide 2 mg in type 2 diabetes: TRANSCEND-T2D-2, the first randomized Phase 3 head-to-head (Lilly topline, Oct 28, 2026), explained alongside the peer-reviewed retatrutide evidence
pieces.angle:
Lane C (log 'lane: C'), 8–12 min, 14:00 ET. First sentence answers the title with a 'you' scenario: 'You have type 2 diabetes and you're on semaglutide. In the first head-to-head trial, retatrutide lowered A1C and weight more, but more people stopped it because of side effects.' News figures, all credited 'Lilly, Oct 28, 2026; company-reported, not yet peer-reviewed; open-label; if everyone stayed on treatment':
- 1,298 adults with type 2 diabetes on metformin, with or without an SGLT2 inhibitor; baseline A1C 7.0–10.5%; 80 weeks; 2:2:1 randomization (per-arm n from the release).
- A1C −2.2 points on retatrutide 9 mg and 12 mg vs −1.8 on semaglutide 2 mg. Give mmol/mol only if the release supports it.
- Weight −19.5% / −20.9% vs −9.4%.
- Side effects, each with its semaglutide rate: diarrhoea, nausea and vomiting per arm; stopping because of side effects 4.8% / 7.9% vs 2.7%; dysesthesia 4.8% / 6.5% vs 2.7%.
The body rests on settled evidence:
(1) What is retatrutide? The GIP, GLP-1 and glucagon receptors explained (peer-reviewed mechanism sources).
(2) What did this trial actually test? Open-label design and what the 'stayed on treatment' measure means. Never say 'estimand'.
(3) How do the results compare with retatrutide's earlier trials? TRIUMPH-2 (Lancet: 1,152 adults with type 2 diabetes and obesity or overweight, 80 weeks, vs placebo) and TRANSCEND-T2D-1 (Lancet, 40 weeks, vs placebo), each labelled as a separate trial.
(4) Why do people with type 2 diabetes lose less weight on these drugs? Separate trials, not head-to-head.
(5) What is dysesthesia? Say only what's confirmed, and that the cause isn't known.
(6) Is retatrutide approved? Investigational, not approved by the FDA, MHRA, Health Canada or TGA as of Oct 29, 2026. Lilly says it plans to file in Q1 2027, and a plan to file isn't approval.
(7) What does this mean if you're on semaglutide now? Nothing changes today. 'Don't switch, stop or change your medicines on your own.'
No 'up to 60 pounds' framing and no 'beat' verdict beyond the reported numbers. Never mention online or research-peptide sources; for approved options or a clinical trial, ask a prescriber. Re-hook every 45–75 s. One subscribe ask, after the side-effects payoff. Include 'Not personal advice' and the full prescriber line. Ending: 'There's a video I'd watch next, linked in the description.' Thumbnail: 4 words or fewer, reaction layout with one labelled character (e.g. 'First Real Matchup'), not big-number.
pieces.working_title: Retatrutide vs Semaglutide: First Head-to-Head Results
pieces.why: Meets every Lane C rule: public within 48 h, a named next-gen drug, a randomized efficacy number and a semaglutide arm. It's the EloraTZP pattern that earned about 54% of our watch time, with the body built on peer-reviewed retatrutide trials so it holds up at fact-check.

pieces.topic: Tirzepatide and the pancreas: how often pancreatitis showed up in randomized trials, what adverse-event databases can and can't tell us, and the label's warning signs (scoping review, Diabetes Metab Syndr Obes, Oct 23, 2026)
pieces.angle: Calm 'honest uncertainty' Short, 170 words or fewer. Open with: 'Worried about your pancreas on tirzepatide? In randomized trials in people with obesity, pancreatitis was uncommon.' Fact 1: a scoping review (Diabetes, Metabolic Syndrome and Obesity, Oct 23, 2026) looked at 11 trials. Five reported pancreatitis, at rates from 0.2% (3 of 1,896 people) to 3.7%, and that 3.7% was 1 person in a trial of 27. Say 'in obesity trials' and don't apply it to type 2 diabetes. Fact 2: adverse-event report databases (FAERS, EudraVigilance) collect reports, but they can't tell you how often something happens. The authors call for standardized reporting. Warning signs, in label wording: severe stomach-area pain that won't go away, with or without vomiting, which may spread to your back. Then: 'contact your healthcare provider right away.' One line: nausea and diarrhoea are common. At most one gallbladder clause. Add 'Don't stop or change your medicines on your own', 'Not personal advice' and the full prescriber line. End with 'Full breakdown on our channel, link in the description.' No scare visuals and no emoji.
pieces.working_title: Tirzepatide and Your Pancreas: What the Trials Show #shorts
pieces.why: Body-worry Shorts with tirzepatide in the title are our best Short format on YouTube (bones 237, nausea 153). A fresh Oct 23 review that no consumer outlet has covered yet gives it a new fact. | fact-check: Source confirmed: Kutsyba, Raj and van der Berg, 'Pancreatic and Gallbladder Adverse Events Associated with Tirzepatide in Obesity Management', Diabetes Metab Syndr Obes, Oct 23, 2026, doi 10.2147/DMSO.S637243. It is a scoping review of 11 RCTs, but only 5 of them reported pancreatitis. Rates ranged from 0.2% (3 of 1,896) to 3.7% (1 of 27). The 3.7% upper end is a single person in a 27-person trial. The review covers obesity only and left out studies done only in type 2 diabetes. Pancreatic and gallbladder events were reported more often in FAERS and EudraVigilance than in the trials. The authors call for vigilant monitoring and standardized reporting. Saying '0.2–3.7% across 11 trials' would misstate this. Also drop 'follow for more': the shared Shorts ending is 'Full breakdown on our channel, link in the description.'

pieces.topic: Food noise on tirzepatide: why cravings can go quiet, and why Halloween candy may feel different (Psychiatric Times, Oct 28, 2026)
pieces.angle: 13:00 Halloween Short, 170 words or fewer. Open with: 'Halloween candy not calling your name on tirzepatide? There may be biology behind that.' Use a peer-reviewed review for how GLP-1 signals act on the brain's appetite and reward areas, labelling animal findings 'in mice' or 'in rats' and human findings 'in people'. Honest line: 'One case report, in a single person, found tirzepatide quieted craving-linked brain activity, but it came back after about five months (Nature Medicine, 2025). That's early research, not proof.' Call it 'a case report in one person', never a study. Habits: eat slowly, stop when comfortably full, and enjoy a treat without guilt. GI line: very sweet or greasy treats may sit less well. No restriction, 'cure' or binge-eating treatment language. Add 'Not personal advice' and the full prescriber line. Loop ending. Don't cite Psychiatric Times.
pieces.working_title: Tirzepatide and Food Noise: Why Halloween Candy Feels Different #shorts
pieces.why: 'Food noise' is one of the most searched GLP-1 phrases, and Halloween is 2 days away. This replaces the usual 13:00 head-to-head because no fresh tirzepatide trial is available, and the retatrutide trial is already used by S3 under the one-trial-per-week rule. | fact-check: I couldn't find the cited Psychiatric Times article from Oct 28, 2026, so don't cite it. The 'small, early tirzepatide study' is really a single-patient case report. Shivacharan et al., Nature Medicine, Nov 17, 2025 (Penn Medicine), recorded brain activity through implanted electrodes in 4 trial participants, but the tirzepatide finding comes from 1 woman. Her craving-linked reward-centre (nucleus accumbens) activity and food preoccupation went quiet at her full dose, then came back after about 5 months. Calling it a 'study' with a group size would overstate it. The authors warn the drugs aren't a fix for binge eating 'in their current form', so make no binge-eating treatment claims. No trial has tested Halloween candy specifically, so frame that part as 'may'. Brain-reward mechanism findings are mostly from animals; label them 'in mice' or 'in rats'.

pieces.topic: What is 'dysesthesia', the retatrutide side effect in the new head-to-head trial? How often it happened against semaglutide 2 mg (TRANSCEND-T2D-2, Lilly, Oct 28, 2026)
pieces.angle: 20:00 funnel Short (Exp D) and spin-off of L1. It asks one fresh question rather than re-cutting the long-form. Answer within 10 s: 'Dysesthesia means odd skin sensations, like tingling or burning. In Lilly's new trial in type 2 diabetes, it was reported in 4.8% on retatrutide 9 mg and 6.5% on 12 mg, versus 2.7% on semaglutide 2 mg, over 80 weeks.' Credit it 'Lilly, Oct 28, 2026; company-reported, not yet peer-reviewed; open-label'. Use numbers that match L1's verified script exactly. Second fact: more people stopped retatrutide because of side effects (4.8% / 7.9% vs 2.7%), while stomach side effects were broadly similar to semaglutide. Give one per-arm nausea figure. Honest uncertainty: the cause isn't known. Status: investigational, not approved anywhere as of Oct 29, 2026. Never mention online products; for approved options or a clinical trial, ask a prescriber. 'Don't switch, stop or change your medicines on your own.' 'Not personal advice' plus the prescriber line. Last spoken line: 'Full breakdown on our channel, link in the description.' No spoken titles. 170 words or fewer. Mix at 0.02 or lower.
pieces.working_title: Retatrutide Side Effects: What Is Dysesthesia? #shorts
pieces.why: Spin-off of L1 (the Exp D funnel to today's Lane C video). Retatrutide Shorts with new Phase 3 data get our highest peaks, and almost no creator explains dysesthesia.

pieces.topic: Protein on tirzepatide: how much protein adults losing weight are generally advised to eat, why it matters when appetite drops (keeping lean mass), and practical ways to hit it with smaller meals
pieces.angle:
Keep the title 'Protein on Tirzepatide: How Much and Why', the lane A label, the structure and all the safety lines. Make these changes:

(a) New opening: 'You're eating much less on tirzepatide, so is protein the thing to protect? Yes. The general adult baseline is zero point eight grams per kilogram of body weight a day, and a 2025 advisory from four nutrition and obesity groups suggests eating your protein food first at meals so you're more likely to get enough.' Don't say 'every meal'.

(b) Chapter 2: give the RDA of 0.8 g/kg/day (US National Academies, also quoted in the advisory). Show the kg and lb working, using whole numbers and a sentence of its own for each decimal. Optionally add: 'For people actively losing weight, higher targets of about 1.2 to 1.6 grams per kilogram have been proposed, and experts don't yet agree on which body weight to use, because using your actual weight can overestimate what you need. One practical range they mention is 80 to 120 grams a day.' Attribute it to the 2025 ACLM/ASN/OMA/TOS advisory. Never say 'you should eat X g' and never say 'recommended for tirzepatide users'. Add: 'Very high intakes, around 2 grams per kilogram or more for a long time, aren't advised. A registered dietitian can set your number.'

(c) Chapter 3: 'protein first' is the advisory's suggestion. Call it 'recommended', never 'proven on tirzepatide'.

(d) Chapter 5: food first. Then: 'The advisory says shakes, bars and fortified foods can help some people reach their protein target.' Replace the 'not shown to protect muscle' line with: 'There's no product the advisory recommends for protecting muscle. Protein plus strength training is the combination it highlights.' No brand names or product shots.

(e) GI line, credited to the advisory: 'Nausea, diarrhoea and constipation are common. Smaller, more frequent meals and avoiding fatty foods, especially early on, can help.' 'Eating slowly' may stay as our own tip with no source tag.

(f) Chapter 6: quote the advisory's point that protein alone is likely not enough to keep muscle without strength training, then give 2 or more days a week of muscle-strengthening (WHO / US Physical Activity Guidelines), started gently.

(g) Chapter 7, check with a clinician first: kidney disease or risk of it, being told to limit protein or fluids, pregnancy, and anyone with a history of disordered eating, who should set targets with their care team rather than track numbers. Keep 'consider asking for a registered dietitian referral'.

(h) Thanksgiving plate: frame it as 'build the plate around turkey or another protein you enjoy, then whatever else you like'. No guilt, no 'earn it', no foods labelled bad, no calorie talk.

(i) DXA chapter: as written (160 scanned; 124 on tirzepatide, all doses pooled, vs 36 on placebo; 72 weeks; no diabetes; about 75% fat / about 25% lean; lean mass isn't pure muscle).

No drug dose numbers anywhere. Ending: 'There's a video I'd watch next, linked in the description.' Sources: Mozaffarian et al., Obesity 2025, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12304835/; Look et al., Diabetes Obes Metab 2025; WHO physical activity guidelines; US Physical Activity Guidelines.
pieces.working_title: Protein on Tirzepatide: How Much and Why
pieces.why:
Next unmade Lane A slot in the growth playbook. Practical tirzepatide long-forms earn about 2.4× the channel's median watch minutes, the topic rests on settled guideline sources that are easy to fact-check, Thanksgiving gives it a hook, and it doesn't overlap with today's Shorts. | fact-check: This is a good Lane A topic. It sits in an allowed pillar, nutrition guidance isn't drug dosing, and the population and DXA substudy figures match the channel's verified facts (Look et al., Diabetes Obes Metab 2025). I checked the 2025 joint advisory (Mozaffarian et al., 'Nutritional priorities to support GLP-1 therapy for obesity', ACLM/ASN/OMA/TOS, published together in Obesity, AJCN, Am J Lifestyle Med and Obesity Pillars; full text at PMC12304835). Four parts of the angle don't match what it actually says:
(1) The opening line says 'nutrition groups suggest putting a protein food at every meal'. The advisory never says 'every meal'. Its words are 'Protein-rich foods can be consumed first in a meal to increase the likelihood of sufficient consumption.'
(2) The higher range does exist, but it is hedged: 'Higher targets, such as 1.2–1.6 g/kg/day, have also been proposed.' The advisory also says it's unclear whether to use actual, adjusted/ideal body weight or fat-free mass, because actual weight 'can significantly overestimate protein requirements'. It offers an absolute target, '80–120 g/day ... may enhance adherence', and says prolonged intake at or above 2 g/kg/day 'should be avoided'. If the higher range is used, it must keep 'have been proposed' and the body-weight caveat.
(3) Chapter 5's supplement claim can't go out unsourced as 'our own summary'. It is a factual claim about the evidence, and the advisory actually says 'Some individuals can meet protein targets by supplementing with high-protein shakes, bars, and other fortified products.'
(4) 'Eating slowly' isn't in the advisory. Its GI advice is 'Smaller, more frequent meals and avoiding fatty or high fiber foods during the first few days of treatment can help alleviate symptoms.'
The advisory also says protein alone is 'likely inadequate' to keep muscle without resistance training. That supports chapter 6. On kidneys, it says people with or at risk of kidney problems should get advice on avoiding dehydration and have kidney function monitored. Two safety gaps: there's no eating-disorder caveat, and the Thanksgiving segment could slip into guilt framing. The title (40 characters, drug first, pays off), the 'Enough Protein?' thumbnail and the reaction layout are all fine.
